message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything, starting with tomorrow's route.

## Route and timeline: B → A → C

This is the **only order that works**:
- **A before B is impossible.** A's earliest delivery is 09:00, so unloading ends at 09:15, and the 25-minute drive reaches B at 09:40, after it opens.
- **C can't come first,** because it accepts nothing before 11:00.

| Time | What happens |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive **B**, unload |
| 09:05 | Leave B (done before the 09:30 opening ✓) |
| 09:30 | Arrive **A**, unload (within the 09:00–10:00 window ✓) |
| 09:45 | Leave A |
| 10:25 | Arrive at C's area. **30-minute break** 10:25–10:55, then wait 5 min |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C** (no earlier than 11:00 ✓) |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| 12:00 | **Back at depot** ✓ |

The break can go wherever suits the driver: after A, or while waiting near C. Either way there's 35 minutes of slack before C opens.

**The catch: he gets back at exactly 12:00, with no slack.** This doesn't depend on the order or the break. C can't start before 11:00, unloading takes 15 minutes, and the drive back is 45. Any delay at C, such as waiting for someone to sign or a tricky carry, makes him late. Two ways to buy some margin:
- **Ask C whether they could accept at 10:45**, or have the delivery ready to go at exactly 11:00.
- **Check whether "back by 12:00" can flex** by 10–15 minutes tomorrow.

It's also worth confirming that someone will be at shop B to receive the delivery at 08:50, before it opens.

## Van name ideas

- **The Dovetail Express**
- **Van Gogh**
- **Chester Drawers**
- **The Veneer Machine**
- **Polly Shing**
- **Old Faithful**

## Friendlier arrival text

> Hi [Name], your driver [Driver] is on the way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition.** Look for any new scratches, dents or chips compared with how it left the workshop. Photograph it in place.
2. **Function.** Open and close drawers and doors, check handles and hardware are secure, and make sure it stands level without wobbling.
3. **Completeness.** Hand over all keys, shelves, fittings and loose parts, and check the customer is happy with where it's been placed.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed by default:** have the customer sign on a phone or tablet, take a photo, and email the record automatically. It's faster, it can't get lost, and it gives you a timestamped record if there's ever a dispute. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer them or don't use email.

## "Proof of delivery," in a line

> **Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, photo and time, showing that the item was handed over in good condition to the right person at the right address.**

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] is due tomorrow between [9:00] and [10:00]. Reply or call [number] if that's a problem. Thanks!

With a typical name, a business name of about 20 characters and a phone number, this comes to about **145 characters**. If your business name is longer, drop "Thanks!" to stay under 160.

Avoid emojis and curly apostrophes, because they can make phones treat the message as "Unicode." The limit then drops to **70 characters**, and the message gets split. Use plain straight apostrophes.
